full_story_part1.text: Put a phone in a bag and click the lock shut. If only we could lock away classroom problems, too. When the screen goes dark, does learning start by itself? A Japanese teacher, a school budget worker, and a student who works and goes to school all face the same bag. But different alarms go off in each person's mind.

full_story_part2.text: Before class, I mark parts to discuss with my middle school Japanese class. I look at the lesson plan spread across the teacher's desk. I think about where to add a check. It would make sure everyone has put their phone away. I want them to focus on the text, not their screens. But I want to protect more than test scores or a quiet classroom. I want time to hear how other people see things differently. I read the parts I marked again, then suddenly stop. What if all these checks leave less time to read the text that matters? It is my job to keep the lesson moving. I cannot think a quiet classroom is enough.

full_story_part3.text: I check school budgets for the local government. I lay out device costs and papers about learning help on my desk. I mark them with sticky notes. Should money for putting phones away count as spending to help students do better at school? I start writing a note about the budget review, then stop. How can I explain the link between not using phones and learning? The budget cannot make money appear from nowhere. I worry that money for the bags could mean less help for students who need help with learning. At the same time, I still do not know if this cost is needed. I decide how the money is shared. So I cannot avoid explaining why.

full_story_part3_c3.text: We all want to value the time we spend learning. But even when we want the same thing, a wrong choice can cost each of us different things. We also have different amounts of responsibility to take on. One bag cannot hold everyone's idea of what is good. There is power to decide how money is spent. There is power to shape the classroom. And there is the duty to keep daily life going. Even people with little say in decisions have burdens just as heavy. What they need to protect may matter deeply. Still, they may not get to take part in the decision. Before we close the bag, are we shutting out even the acceptance someone has not yet found the words to express?
